article_title: AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning
citation: Wei Wang, Enlin Gu, Antonio Loquercio, Haimin Hu, Rahul Mangharam. (2026). AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25337
title: Learning to Coach (L2C): an RL pipeline combining adaptive blending, a skill-change PFA, and a surrogate reward
description: L2C is the article's trainable coaching framework built on the Coaching Game formalism. Its contributions are "threefold: (i) a closed-loop blending rule that adapts the assistance levelλto the coach's observations of both the physical environment and the learner behavior; (ii) a reformu-lation of theCoaching Gameto a single-agent POMDP, solvable via RL, through a probabilistic model of the coach's causal influence on learner skill; and (iii) a tractable surrogate reward that is provably consistent with the counterfactual V oI objective." A hybrid probabilistic finite-state automaton models skill change on success and failure events with sigmoid rates over skill; the coach policy is trained with PPO against skill improvement and deployed with Bayesian runtime skill inference and multimodal feedback.
requirements: A pretrained expert policy to anchor the blending rule
A learner model expressible as a skill-parameterized policy class
Privileged access to learner skill during simulation training
constraints: The Boltzmann learner model is one tractable choice; the article states accurately modeling skill-conditioned learner behaviors remains an open problem
Verbal and visual cues are predefined and triggered by fixed rules; only assistance modulation of physical control is learned
target_learners: human learners practicing motor skills such as FPV drone racing, mostly novices
target_learning_goals: accelerated development of independent motor-skill competence, measured by unassisted lap time and failure count
examples: Deployed in a 40-minute FPV drone racing coaching session with shared control, verbal instructions, visual cues, and guided re-attempts of failed segments
key_sources: Wei Wang, Enlin Gu, Antonio Loquercio, Haimin Hu, Rahul Mangharam. (2026). AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25337

citation: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311
title: L2 anxiety as a negatively acting affective variable in L2 learning with (non)linguistic moderators
description: The article frames L2 anxiety as an affective variable with a demonstrably negative role in L2 learning, moderated by linguistic and nonlinguistic variables. It states the study "provides firm evidence for both the negative role of L2 anxiety in L2 learning and the moderating effects of a number of (non)linguistic variables." The framework builds on decades of empirical and theoretical attention to L2 anxiety and its relationship with achievement.
requirements: Measurement of both anxiety (various types) and language achievement to estimate the relationship
constraints: Effect sizes vary across achievement measure types, educational levels, target languages, and anxiety types, so the negative association is not uniform
examples: Meta-analysis of 216 correlations yielding a mean r = −.36
key_sources: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311

article_title: Unraveling the nexus among achievement goals, self-efficacy, and motivation regulation and their joint effects on L2 student writers’ writing achievement: a person-based approach
citation: Jianhua Zhang, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Unraveling the nexus among achievement goals, self-efficacy, and motivation regulation and their joint effects on L2 student writers' writing achievement: a person-based approach. Metacognition and Learning (2025) 20:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09434-0
title: A four-profile taxonomy of L2 writing achievement goals grounded in the trichotomous achievement goal model and person-based (latent profile) analysis
description: The article organizes L2 student writers' motivation via the trichotomous achievement goal model (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance) combined with a person-based latent profile approach. Latent profile analysis yielded four profiles labeled, in the article's words, "Low All Goals (LAGs)", "Mastery High (MH)", "Average All Goals (AAGs)", and "High All Goals (HAGs)". The taxonomy is used to test whether self-efficacy, motivation regulation, and writing achievement differ across learner types rather than across variables. Three profiles matched prevalent profiles in Wormington and Linnenbrink-Garcia's (2017) synthesis, which the authors take as supporting cross-contextual stability of goal adoption patterns.
requirements: Requires measures of mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance writing goals (here the adapted Writing Achievement Goals Scale) and latent profile analysis with fit indices (AIC, BIC, aBIC, entropy, LMR-LRT, BLRT).
constraints: Profiles were identified in a convenience sample of tertiary EFL students in Southwest China; the authors note contextual factors in L2 writing may influence how achievement goals are endorsed.
target_learning_goals: L2 writing achievement and motivation regulation in writing
examples: The study assigned 416 students to the four profiles and compared them on self-efficacy, motivation regulation strategies, and writing achievement in two genres.
